heroIntro: Following marital breakdown or divorce in Bangladesh, one of the most stressful bureaucratic battles single mothers encounter is securing a national machine-readable or e-passport for their minor children. Regional passport offices under the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) routinely insist upon the physical presence or a written No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the biological father. When an estranged father maliciously withholds consent, is untraceable, or resides overseas, the child's fundamental right to travel, undergo medical treatment, or pursue education abroad is paralyzed. Under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and established Supreme Court writ precedents, mothers holding physical custody (Hizanat) possess clear legal remedies to compel passport issuance without paternal obstruction.

quickAnswer.title: Can a Divorced Mother Get a Minor Child's Passport Without the Father's Consent?
quickAnswer.text: Yes. While standard administrative passport guidelines request parental consent, a divorced mother who has lawful custody of her child can legally obtain an e-passport without the father's consent. If the father refuses to provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC) or cannot be located, the mother can obtain a legal guardianship or custody certificate from the Family Court under Section 7 and Section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, or petition the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution for a Writ of Mandamus directing the Department of Immigration and Passports to issue the passport in the mother's sole custody.
highlights: Passport offices cannot arbitrarily deny a minor child travel documents if lawful custody is proven.
The biological father's refusal of an NOC does not permanently bar passport issuance.
Family Court guardianship decrees under the 1890 Act supersede administrative objections.
The High Court Division routinely issues writ directions compelling passport issuance for minors.
points: Governing Legislation: Guardians and Wards Act 1890, Bangladesh Passport Order 1973, Family Courts Act 2023.
Custody Distinction: Maternal physical custody (Hizanat) versus paternal legal guardianship (Wilayat).
Judicial Forum: Family Court (Assistant Judge Court) and High Court Division of the Supreme Court.

sections.title: 1. The Bureaucratic Barrier: Why Passport Offices Demand Father's Consent
sections.content:
Under the standard application protocols established by the Department of Immigration and Passports (DIP) in Bangladesh, any passport application submitted on behalf of a minor under 18 years of age requires parental verification. Frontline passport enrolment officers at regional offices (such as Agargaon, Uttara, Jatrabari, or district branches) routinely demand the national identification cards (NID) of both parents alongside an explicit No Objection Certificate (NOC) signed by the father.

When parents have undergone a divorce or separation, this administrative requirement frequently becomes an instrument of harassment. An estranged father may deliberately refuse to sign the NOC, demand that the mother forfeit her pending dower (Denmohar) or past child maintenance in exchange for his signature, or simply vanish and become untraceable.

Because desk officers fear accusations of facilitating child abduction or cross-border custody violations, they often summarily reject the mother's solo application. However, departmental circulars and administrative guidelines are subordinate to statutory law and constitutional protections. A passport is an essential identity document belonging to the citizen child, not a personal asset of the father.

sections.title: 2. Legal Framework: Custody (Hizanat) vs. Guardianship (Wilayat) in Bangladesh
sections.content:
To effectively challenge passport denials, one must understand the crucial legal distinction between custody and legal guardianship under Bangladeshi family jurisprudence. In Muslim personal law, physical custody of a child is known as Hizanat, while legal guardianship over the person and property is termed Wilayat.

Under Hanafi law, the mother is entitled to the custody (Hizanat) of her male child until he completes the age of seven years, and of her female child until puberty. Even after these ages, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has established in a series of landmark judgments that custody does not automatically shift to the father; the primary inquiry remains whether the child's overall welfare is best preserved in the mother's care.

While classical personal law recognizes the father as the natural legal guardian (Wilayat), this status is not absolute. When a father fails in his parental duties, refuses maintenance, or abandons the child, the civil courts have statutory authority under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 to appoint the mother as the sole legal guardian for personal and administrative affairs, including obtaining government identity documents. For broader perspectives on custody principles, consult our guide on child custody laws in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 3. The Paramount Doctrine: Welfare of the Minor in Travel & Education
sections.content:
The cornerstone of Bangladeshi family law regarding children is Section 17 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, which mandates that in appointing or declaring a guardian, the court shall be guided by what appears to be for the welfare of the minor. This statutory principle overrides traditional rigid dogmas.

The Appellate Division and High Court Division have consistently ruled that administrative barriers cannot be used to deprive a child of their welfare, which includes the freedom of movement under Article 36 of the Constitution, access to advanced medical treatment in foreign hospitals, and the pursuit of international schooling or higher education.

When an estranged father uses his refusal to sign a passport application purely as spite or extortion, the courts view this conduct as detrimental to the child's best interests. In such circumstances, judicial authority promptly steps in to override the father's passive veto and ensure that the child's identity documents are promptly released.

sections.title: 4. Procuring a Guardianship Certificate from the Family Court (Act VIII of 1890)
sections.content:
The most permanent and robust civil mechanism for a single mother seeking independent legal authority over her child's documentation is filing a guardianship petition before the Family Court. Under the Family Courts Act 2023, the Family Court (presided over by an Assistant Judge or Senior Assistant Judge) has exclusive original jurisdiction over custody and guardianship matters.

The mother files an application under Section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, naming the biological father as the opposite party. The petition must set out the facts of the divorce, the father's abandonment or refusal to cooperate, and the specific necessity of obtaining an official guardianship decree to facilitate the minor's e-passport application, schooling, and healthcare.

The court issues summons to the father. If the father appears and contests, the court evaluates the evidence focusing strictly on the child's welfare. If the father fails to appear after service of summons, the court proceeds ex parte. Upon being satisfied that the child resides permanently with the mother and that the father has neglected his obligations, the Family Court passes a decree appointing the mother as the legal guardian of the person of the minor, explicitly empowering her to apply for and collect the child's passport.

sections.title: 5. High Court Division Writ Petitions (Article 102) for Urgent Passport Issuance
sections.content:
While a Family Court guardianship proceeding provides a complete adjudication, it can take six to twelve months to conclude. In situations of urgent necessity—such as where the child requires immediate medical surgery abroad, has received a time-sensitive foreign visa or university admission, or the mother must relocate for employment—the High Court Division offers swift constitutional relief.

Under Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, the mother can file a Writ Petition seeking a Writ of Mandamus against the Director General of the Department of Immigration and Passports, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the regional passport officer. The petition asserts that the arbitrary refusal to issue an e-passport violates the child's fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 27 (equality before law), Article 31 (protection of law), and Article 36 (freedom of movement).

Upon hearing preliminary submissions from counsel, the High Court Division bench routinely issues a Rule Nisi accompanied by an interim mandatory direction instructing the passport authorities to accept the mother's application without the father's NOC and deliver the e-passport within a specified period (typically 7 to 15 days). This constitutional mechanism has empowered hundreds of single mothers to secure emergency travel papers without submitting to paternal coercion. For specialized insights, review our practice overview on Supreme Court writ litigation.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Administrative Obstacles, Legal Options & Timelines
sections.content:
Single mothers evaluating their options can compare the procedural routes, required documentation, and expected timelines in the following comparative matrix:

Procedural Pathway Primary Authority / Forum Key Prerequisites Estimated Resolution Time
Mutual Consent / Father's NOC Regional Passport Office (DIP) Signed standard NOC, father's NID copy, joint presence if requested Standard delivery (7 to 21 days)
Family Court Guardianship Suit Family Court (Assistant Judge) Divorce proof, birth certificate, evidence of father's refusal/neglect 4 to 9 months (permanent decree)

Administrative Appeal to DIP DG Director General, Passports (Agargaon) Formal legal notice, divorce papers, police verification report 1 to 2 months (discretionary)

sections.title: 7. Taking the Child Abroad: Preventing Airport Offloading and Travel Injunctions
sections.content:
Procuring the physical e-passport is only the first hurdle; single mothers planning to take their child abroad for permanent relocation, schooling, or holidays must also protect against potential border interception. In bitter matrimonial disputes, fathers frequently file applications before the Family Court seeking an order of temporary injunction restraining the mother from removing the child from Bangladesh.

Alternatively, some fathers lodge police General Diaries or file false abduction petitions under Section 363 of the Penal Code 1860, resulting in the child's name being placed on the immigration watchlist at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA). To prevent traumatic offloading at the departure gate, mothers should obtain a clear declaration from the Family Court permitting foreign travel.

When the Family Court or High Court authorizes international travel, it may require the mother to submit an undertaking or provide reasonable visitation access through digital video conferencing during overseas stays. Carrying certified copies of the court judgment, guardianship order, and birth certificate during international transit provides ironclad legal immunity at immigration counters. For broader guidance on travel bans, see our analysis on travel bans and airport offload challenges in Bangladesh.

sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Mother Overcoming Father's Malicious Passport Block
sections.content:
To understand how this dual judicial remedy operates in practice, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A divorced mother residing in Uttara, Dhaka, had custody of her eight-year-old daughter following a finalized divorce in 2023. The mother secured a prestigious academic fellowship in Canada and prepared to relocate with her daughter. When she visited the regional passport office to renew her daughter's expiring passport, the assistant director refused to process the biometrics, stating that under departmental directives, a divorced mother could not renew a minor's passport without the father's in-person signature or a notarized NOC.

The biological father, who had contributed zero maintenance for three years, explicitly refused to sign the NOC unless the mother relinquished her pending 15 Lakh BDT dower claim. Faced with an impending visa deadline, the mother retained a Supreme Court advocate.

The advocate filed a Writ Petition under Article 102 before the High Court Division, demonstrating that the child's fundamental right to education and travel was being held hostage for private financial extortion. The High Court issued an immediate interim directive commanding the Director General of Immigration and Passports to enroll the child's biometrics and issue the e-passport within ten working days based solely on the mother's guardianship. Concurrently, the Family Court finalized her legal guardianship decree, enabling the mother and child to travel abroad without impediment.

sections.title: 9. Practical Document Checklist for Divorced Mothers Applying for Passports
sections.content:
Single mothers preparing to navigate passport applications or judicial proceedings should compile a meticulous evidentiary dossier before approaching authorities:

  • Child's Official Birth Registration: Secure an online-verified, 17-digit digital Birth Registration Certificate (BRC) from the local City Corporation or Union Parishad.
  • Proof of Finalized Divorce: Procure the certified Talaqnama and the final Failure of Reconciliation Certificate issued by the City Corporation or Union Parishad Chairman under Section 7 MFLO.
  • Custody & Maintenance Records: Compile any Family Court orders, compromise deeds (Solenama), or bank records demonstrating that the mother is the primary custodian and financial provider.
  • Proof of Father's Refusal or Absence: Maintain copies of registered legal notices sent to the father requesting cooperation, WhatsApp or email refusals, or police GDs confirming that his whereabouts are unknown.
  • Evidence of Travel Necessity: Keep school admission letters, medical diagnosis reports, foreign visa appointment confirmations, or employment relocation contracts.

faqs.question: Can a mother get a passport for her child without the father's consent in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although passport offices routinely ask for the father's NOC, a divorced mother can obtain the child's passport by securing a guardianship decree from the Family Court under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, or by obtaining an interim direction from the High Court Division via a writ petition.

faqs.question: Why do Bangladeshi passport offices refuse passport applications without the father's NOC?
faqs.answer: Regional passport offices adhere to internal administrative operating rules designed to prevent cross-border parental child abduction. However, these departmental guidelines cannot override statutory family court decrees or constitutional rights.

faqs.question: What is the difference between custody (Hizanat) and guardianship (Wilayat)?
faqs.answer: Custody (Hizanat) refers to the day-to-day physical care and living arrangement of the child, which typically resides with the mother. Guardianship (Wilayat) relates to legal authority over the child's person and property, which the Family Court can grant to the mother.

faqs.question: How long does it take to obtain a Family Court guardianship decree for a child passport?
faqs.answer: A standard guardianship case under Section 10 of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 generally takes four to nine months, depending on court schedules and whether the biological father contests the proceedings.

faqs.question: What is the fastest way to get a child passport if the mother has an urgent travel deadline?
faqs.answer: The fastest mechanism is filing a Writ of Mandamus before the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. Upon proof of urgency (such as foreign medical treatment or visa deadlines), the bench can issue an interim order within two to four weeks.

faqs.question: Can a father stop a divorced mother from taking their child out of Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: A father can file an application for an injunction in the Family Court to restrict international travel. However, courts will only grant a restriction if travel is shown to be harmful to the child's welfare; courts routinely allow travel for education and healthcare.

faqs.question: What happens if the biological father cannot be traced or lives abroad without contact?
faqs.answer: If the father's whereabouts are unknown, the mother can file a police GD and initiate a Family Court guardianship case where summons will be served via national newspaper publication, leading to an ex parte decree appointing her legal guardian.

faqs.question: Does having physical custody automatically allow a mother to renew a minor's e-passport?
faqs.answer: Physical custody alone is often disputed by passport desk officers. Having a formalized Family Court guardianship decree or High Court writ direction provides an indisputable legal instrument that compels passport officers to issue or renew the document.
